messages.content: You are a Minecraft DSL Compiler. Translate the architectural plan into raw DSL code.

I am analyzing the spatial blueprint for 'Suburban House #1'. As the Master Teacher, I will break down the raw coordinates into a logical, architectural sequence so you can visualize the structure before placing a single block.

1. Footprint Analysis
I am working with a bounding box that is 13 blocks wide (X=0 to 12), 23 blocks deep (Z=0 to 22), and 14 blocks tall (Y=0 to 13). This is a tiered, hollow structure. The footprint is an asymmetrical L-shape: the main two-story living space occupies the left and center, while a single-story garage extension projects forward on the right side. 

2. Material Strategy
I will use a realistic, modern suburban palette:
- Grass Block (A) and Dirt (B): I will use these to ground the build, creating the yard and the foundational footprint.
- Oak Planks (C): I will use this as my primary warm material for interior floors and exterior siding.
- Stone (E): I will use this for structural integrity—foundations, structural pillars, and roof trimming.
- Stone Slab (D): I will use these for paved driveways, walkways, and smooth roof peaks.
- Quartz Block (F): I will use this bright, clean material specifically for the garage door and a modern side-awning.
- Air (.): I will use this to carve out the hollow interior, windows, and doors.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
I will now build this house layer by layer, explaining my architectural decisions.

Y=0: The Foundation and Landscaping
I am laying the groundwork. I will surround the property with Grass. I will use Dirt to outline the exact footprint of the house to prevent grass from growing inside. I will fill the interior ground floor with Oak Planks. On the right side (X=9 to 11), I will lay down Stone and Stone Slabs to pour a driveway. On the left, I will lay a smaller Stone walkway leading to a side entrance.

Y=1 to Y=3: The First Floor Walls
I am raising the ground floor. At Y=1, I will use a solid ring of Stone to create a sturdy base trim. Moving up to Y=2 and Y=3, I will transition the main walls to Oak Planks, framed by Stone pillars at the corners. I will intentionally leave gaps in these walls to serve as windows and doors. On the right side, facing the driveway, I will place a wide wall of Quartz blocks—this represents a clean, white, paneled garage door.

Y=4: The First Floor Ceiling and Awnings
I am capping the first floor. I will fill the interior ceiling with Oak Planks. I will use Stone to create a trim that overhangs the walls slightly. On the left side of the house, I will extend a layer of Quartz and Stone outward. I am doing this to create a modern, flat awning that provides shade over the side walkway.

Y=5 to Y=7: The Second Floor Walls
I am starting the second story. I will step the footprint inward, leaving the garage section on the right exposed (it will only be one story). I will build the second-story walls using the same Oak Plank siding and Stone corner-pillar motif as the first floor. At Y=7, I will add Stone Slabs on the left side to act as window sills or a Juliet balcony railing.

Y=8: The Lower Roof and Second Floor Ceiling
I am capping the second floor with Oak Planks and Stone. Simultaneously, I am addressing the exposed garage roof projecting to the front. I will place a line of Stone Slabs down the center of the garage section to begin forming a gentle, sloped lower roof.

Y=9 to Y=11: The Main Pitched Roof
I am constructing the primary roof over the two-story section. I will not use stairs; instead, I will use a tiered block method. Layer by layer, I will step the Stone and Oak Planks inward by one block on all sides. This creates a classic, sturdy pyramidal/A-frame roof slope. By Y=11, the roof has narrowed to a small cross-shape of Stone blocks.

Y=12: The Roof Peak
I am finishing the structure. I will place a single, straight line of Stone Slabs running down the very center of the main roof (X=7). I am using slabs here to give the roof ridge a smooth, finished cap rather than a jagged blocky edge.

Y=13: The Sky
I will leave this layer entirely as Air. This ensures the top of the roof has breathing room and completes the bounding box cleanly. 

By following this logic, I have transformed a grid of letters into a fully realized, two-story suburban home with an attached garage, side awning, and a pitched roof.
You are a Minecraft DSL Compiler. Translate the architectural plan into raw DSL code.

As the Master Teacher, I will guide you through the spatial rationale for the structure designated 'Sandstone House Nr3'. Although the name implies sandstone, I will adapt our material strategy to use standard Stone as our primary masonry, creating a sturdy, brutalist-inspired blockhouse with a softer, shaded eastern patio. 

1. Footprint Analysis
I will work within a total bounding box of 19 blocks wide (X), 11 blocks deep (Z), and 8 blocks tall (Y=0 to Y=7). The core structure is a rectangular, hollow stone building measuring 11x7 blocks. Attached to the eastern side of this main building, I will construct a tiered, slanted awning that covers an outdoor patio area. The building features a flat, open-air roof rather than a traditional pitched roof.

2. Material Strategy
I will use Stone (B) for the thick, load-bearing exterior walls and the roof parapet. I will use Oak Planks (E) for the interior flooring to provide a warm, habitable contrast to the cold stone. Oak Logs (C) are crucial here; I will use them structurally as patio pillars, door/window frames, and as exposed floor joists that protrude from the masonry. I will use White Wool (F) to simulate a lightweight, stretched canvas awning over the patio. Finally, Grass (A) and Dirt (D) will serve as our natural foundation.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic

Layer Y=0 (Foundation & Ground Floor)
I will begin by laying a canvas of Grass. From X=2 to X=12 and Z=2 to Z=8, I will map out the 11x7 rectangular footprint of the house. I will outline this in Stone and fill the interior (X=3 to X=11) with Oak Planks to create the ground floor. On the far eastern edge (X=16), I will place two Dirt blocks at Z=2 and Z=8. These will act as the grounded footings for my patio pillars.

Layers Y=1 to Y=3 (First Floor Walls & Patio Pillars)
I will raise the Stone walls of the house, keeping the interior completely hollow. On the northern wall (Z=2), I will integrate Oak Logs into the stone to frame a sturdy entrance or large window. Out on the patio, I will build two freestanding Oak Log pillars on top of the dirt footings at X=16, raising them up three blocks high. 

Layer Y=4 (Wall Capping & Awning Base)
I will cap the first-floor stone walls. Now, I must begin the patio roof. I will string a solid line of White Wool from Z=2 to Z=8 at X=16, resting directly on top of the two oak pillars. This forms the lowest edge of our canvas awning.

Layer Y=5 (Exposed Joists & Awning Slant)
I will create a complex structural transition layer here. Instead of solid stone, I will lay a grid of Oak Logs running north-to-south through the walls. I will allow these logs to protrude one block outside the stone walls (at Z=1 and Z=9) to create rugged, exposed architectural corbels. To the east, I will step the White Wool awning one block inward (west) to X=15. This upward and inward shift is how I will create the diagonal slant of the canvas roof.

Layer Y=6 (Second Floor & Awning Slant)
Inside the stone walls, I will lay down a massive platform of Oak Planks to serve as the floor for the second story (or the flat roof deck). Outside, I will step the White Wool awning inward once again to X=14, continuing its diagonal trajectory toward the main building.

Layer Y=7 (Parapet & Awning Apex)
I will build a final, one-block-high Stone wall around the perimeter of the Oak Plank floor. This acts as a safety parapet for the flat roof. I will place the final row of White Wool at X=13. This perfectly connects the highest point of the slanted canvas awning directly to the eastern stone wall of the house.

Layers Y=8 & Y=9 (Clearance)
I will leave these layers completely empty. The structure tops out at the Y=7 parapet, leaving the sky open above the flat roof. 

By following this logic, you should now clearly visualize a two-story flat-roofed stone house with exposed wooden joists, featuring a stretched white canvas tent-roof leaning against its eastern wall.

Listen closely, my student. Today we are examining a structure named 'testtt'. At first glance, you might be confused by the reference code, but this is a crucial lesson in Minecraft architecture: the concept of the void, or the test schematic. I will break down my spatial rationale for this unique blueprint so you can visualize exactly what we are doing.

First, I will analyze the footprint. What are the X, Y, and Z dimensions? Because the palette is completely empty, the dimensions are effectively null, or a defined bounding box containing absolutely nothing. Is it hollow, solid, or tiered? It is the ultimate hollow structure—a pure vacuum. I will use this footprint to understand how our spatial tools handle empty space and coordinate boundaries without the interference of physical blocks.

Next, I must explain my material strategy. In a standard build, I would ask myself: Why use Stone for the base? Why place Glass here? I would normally choose Stone for a heavy, grounded foundation and Glass to invite natural light and provide visibility. However, for 'testtt', my material choice is deliberate nothingness. I will use an empty palette because this is a diagnostic tool. I should use this schematic not to build, but to test our exporting software, or perhaps to act as a 3D "eraser" to clear a plot of land back to pure air. 

Now, I will walk you through the construction sequence, layer by layer, so you understand the logic of the void.
At Y=0, I am establishing the foundation of our test. Instead of laying cobblestone or dirt, I am intentionally leaving this layer blank. I will use this empty layer to ensure our baseline coordinates are registering correctly in the world without block interference. 
At Y=1, I am continuing the void. I will ensure no blocks obstruct this space, maintaining a sterile environment.
At Y=4, where I might normally be starting a roof overhang to provide shade, I am instead verifying that the upper bounds of our test region remain completely clear. I should keep every subsequent layer entirely free of blocks. The logical purpose of this entire sequence is to guarantee a perfectly empty volume of space.

By studying 'testtt', I want you to visualize not a building, but the canvas itself. I will always remember that before I can construct grand castles and complex geometric shapes, I must first understand how to define, select, and control empty space.

Welcome, student. Today we are constructing a 'Chicken'. This is not just a random assortment of blocks; it is a carefully sculpted, textured organic shape. I will guide you through my spatial reasoning so you can visualize the bird before placing a single block.

Footprint Analysis:
I will define our workspace. The bounding box is 12 blocks long on the X-axis (front-to-back), 14 blocks high on the Y-axis, and 8 blocks wide on the Z-axis (side-to-side). I will build this as a solid structure, utilizing a dense core to support the overhanging head and tail, while keeping the extremities thin and delicate. The chicken will be facing the positive X direction (rightwards).

Material Strategy:
I have a limited, monochromatic palette: White Wool, Quartz Block, and Stone. I will use White Wool and Quartz to create the bright, fluffy appearance of the chicken's feathers. I will use Stone for two specific reasons: first, as a structural filler for the unseen internal core to save on decorative materials, and second, mixed into the outer layer to provide shading, depth, and a ruffled, dithered texture to the plumage. 

Construction Sequence & Logic:

At Y=0, I will begin with the feet. I need a stable, grounded base, so I will lay down two flat, webbed shapes using White Wool. One foot spans Z=1 to Z=3, and the other Z=4 to Z=6. I will concentrate these around X=3 to X=5, giving the chicken a firm stance.

At Y=1 through Y=3, I will construct the legs. Chickens have thin, spindly legs, so I will build two single-block columns of White Wool rising straight up from the center of each foot at X=3 (specifically at Z=2 and Z=5). This gives the bird its characteristic height off the ground.

At Y=4 and Y=5, I will start the underbelly of the main body. I will create a large, solid mass from X=1 to X=8. To be efficient, I will fill the center entirely with Stone. For the visible exterior, I will dither White Wool, Quartz, and Stone to simulate the shadows and ruffled feathers underneath the bird.

At Y=6 and Y=7, I will expand the body to its maximum width to form the wings. I will push the outer shell outward into Z=0 and Z=7, creating a distinct bulge on the sides. I will keep the core solid Stone, ensuring I do not waste textured blocks where they cannot be seen.

At Y=8 and Y=9, I will round off the top of the back and begin the transition to the neck and tail. At the rear (X=1), I will taper the blocks to suggest tail feathers. At the front (X=7 to X=10), I will extend the structure outward and upward to form the thick base of the neck, leaning into the positive X direction.

At Y=10 and Y=11, I will leave the main body behind and focus entirely on the head. I will build a dense, textured block from X=7 to X=11, centered over the neck. The blocks extending all the way to X=11 will serve as the beak, jutting sharply forward.

At Y=12 and Y=13, I will complete the build by adding the comb. I will place a narrow, jagged ridge of blocks on top of the head from X=7 to X=9, tapering off at the very top (Y=13) to give the chicken its iconic silhouette. 

By following this logic, I ensure the structure is stable, the materials are used efficiently to create a feathered texture, and the final shape perfectly captures the anatomical essence of a chicken.

You are a Minecraft DSL Compiler. Translate the architectural plan into raw DSL code.

Footprint Analysis:
I will begin by analyzing the overall dimensions of this build. The footprint is 5 blocks wide (X=0 to 4), 13 blocks long (Z=0 to 12), and 4 blocks tall (Y=0 to 3). This is a specialized, tiered vehicle structure. To orient ourselves, Z=12 is the front of the truck, and Z=0 is the rear. The front section (Z=8 to Z=11) forms a solid, enclosed double cab, while the rear section (Z=0 to Z=7) is a flatbed housing a central, backward-extending crane mechanism. 

Material Strategy:
I must choose materials that convey heavy industry and utility. 
- Stone (B) is my primary structural material. I will use it for the heavy chassis, the tires, the engine block, and the crane's main pillar. It gives the truck a rugged, unyielding feel.
- Stone Slabs (A) will be used for detailing and half-height elements. I will use them for the undercarriage drive shaft, the flatbed surface, the cab's roof, and the extending arm of the crane to keep the profile sleek rather than overly bulky.
- Glass (D) will be used for the cab's windshield, side, and rear windows, providing the driver with 360-degree visibility.
- White Stained Glass (E) will act as emergency flashing light bars mounted on the roof.
- Torches (C) will be placed at the very front bumper to serve as headlights.

Construction Sequence:

Layer Y=0 (The Undercarriage & Wheels):
I will start by laying out the wheelbase and lower chassis. I need to establish a low but visible ground clearance. At the front (Z=10), I will build a heavy front axle with double wheels using Stone and a central Slab (BBABB). Moving back to Z=7, I will place the outer rear wheels (B.A.B), and at Z=5, I will place inner wheels or transmission gears (.BAB.). I will connect all of these components down the center (X=2) using Stone Slabs to form the drive shaft and lower chassis frame, extending all the way to a rear bumper at Z=2.

Layer Y=1 (The Flatbed & Cab Base):
Moving up, I will build the main body of the truck. At the very front (Z=12), I will place two Torches to act as the truck's headlights. Just behind this, I will construct the solid floor and lower engine block of the double cab using Stone. For the rear section (Z=2 to Z=6), I will build the outer edges of the flatbed using Stone, leaving the center hollow to accommodate the base mechanics of the crane. At Z=7, I will place a solid, 5-block-wide row of Stone (BBBBB). This acts as the heavy structural mounting point for the crane and the truck's outriggers.

Layer Y=2 (The Cab Windows & Crane Pivot):
Now I will enclose the passenger cabin and start the crane's vertical build. For the double cab (Z=8 to Z=11), I will use Glass blocks to create a large front windshield, side windows, and a rear window. I will separate these glass panes with Stone blocks to act as the cab's structural pillars. Behind the cab, at Z=7, I will place a single central Stone block to serve as the heavy pivot joint for the crane. I will use Stone Slabs to build the protective side rails of the flatbed, and I will place a single Stone Slab floating out the back at Z=0 to represent the resting hook of the crane.

Layer Y=3 (The Roof & Crane Arm):
Finally, I will cap the vehicle and extend the crane arm. I will roof the double cab using Stone Slabs to maintain a sleek, aerodynamic profile. At Z=10 on the roof, I will place White Stained Glass blocks on the left and right edges to serve as emergency light bars, with a Stone block in the center to mount them. For the crane, I will build a solid Stone base directly over the pivot (Z=6 and Z=7). From this base, I will extend a long, straight arm of Stone Slabs down the center (X=2) from Z=4 all the way back to Z=1. I will cap the very end of this arm at Z=0 with a solid Stone block to represent the heavy lifting winch and pulley system.

You are a Minecraft DSL Compiler. Translate the architectural plan into raw DSL code.

I am looking at a structure with a 10x7 footprint (10 blocks wide on the X-axis, 7 blocks deep on the Z-axis) that rises 8 blocks high (Y=0 through Y=7). This is a tiered, hollow structure. The base layers are solid to ground the building into the earth, but the middle layers open up to form a cozy, enclosed living space before tapering off into a narrow roof and chimney. 

To build this "poor village house," my material strategy must reflect a humble, rugged lifestyle. I will use dirt and grass blocks for the very bottom layer to embed the house naturally into the surrounding terrain. I will use gravel to create a worn, trodden path leading up to the home. For the architecture itself, I will rely heavily on stone and oak planks. The stone provides a cheap, sturdy defense against the elements, while the oak planks act as patched structural framing, breaking up the cold gray with warm wood. I will use just a single white stained glass block for a modest window, as glass is a luxury. Inside, I will provide only the bare survival necessities: a crafting table, a furnace, a bookshelf, and torches.

Here is how I will construct this building, layer by layer:

At Y=0, I am laying down the sub-foundation. I will fill this layer almost entirely with dirt and grass to match the natural earth. Along the front edge, I will place a couple of cobblestone blocks to act as rugged stepping stones or foundation markers. 

At Y=1, I am building the true foundation and the exterior pathway. I will construct a solid 8x6 stone pad to elevate the floor of the house slightly above the damp ground. On the left side of the footprint, I will lay down a trail of gravel to create a rustic path leading toward the entrance. 

At Y=2, I am starting the lower walls. I will build the perimeter using a mix of stone and oak planks to create a patched, uneven aesthetic typical of a poor village. I will leave the center hollow to form the interior living space. Tucked inside against the wall, I will place a crafting table so the inhabitant can work.

At Y=3, I am raising the mid-walls. I will continue the exact same perimeter pattern of stone and oak planks, ensuring the interior remains hollow so the villager has room to stand. 

At Y=4, I am finishing the upper walls and furnishing the home. I will insert a white stained glass block on the front wall to serve as a small window, letting in a sliver of natural light. Inside the hollow room, I will place a furnace against the back wall for warmth and cooking, and a bookshelf in the corner for a touch of comfort. I will also mount torches on the interior oak frame to illuminate the dark space.

At Y=5, I am starting the roof. I will cap the living space by laying down a flat layer of stone across the top of the walls to form a sturdy ceiling. I will let a few oak planks jut out slightly on the edges to represent crude eaves or exposed structural supports.

At Y=6, I am forming the roof peak. I will build a narrow ridge of stone straight down the center of the ceiling to create a modest pitched roof. Within this ridge, I will place a single cobblestone block to act as the base of a small, crude chimney.

At Y=7, I am completing the build. I will place a single stone block directly on top of the cobblestone from the previous layer. This finishes the chimney, giving this humble village house its final, recognizable silhouette against the sky.

Welcome, student. Today we are engineering a vehicle designated as the 'Brown car'. Do not let the name deceive you into thinking the entire chassis is made of wood; rather, the namesake comes from its exposed, rustic wooden undercarriage that grounds the build. I will guide you through the spatial mathematics of this machine so you can see it in your mind's eye before placing a single block.

Footprint Analysis:
I am working within a bounding box that is 5 blocks wide along the X-axis (X=0 to 4), 10 blocks long along the Z-axis (Z=0 to 9), and 4 blocks tall along the Y-axis (Y=0 to 3). The structure is tiered and highly sculpted. It begins with a narrow underbelly, expands outward to a wide wheelbase, pulls back into a solid rectangular body, and features a hollowed-out central cabin capped by a compact roof. 

Material Strategy:
I will use three specific materials to define the car's anatomy. I will use Oak Planks for the central drive shaft—this provides the 'brown' wooden undertone of the build. I will use Stone heavily for the rugged exterior, forming the thick tires, the heavy bumpers, the solid hood, and the roof. Finally, I will use White Wool for the floorpan and interior lining, providing a soft, insulated contrast to the cold stone exterior.

Construction Sequence:

At Y=0, I am establishing the lowest point of the car, the undercarriage. I will place exactly two Oak Planks in the dead center of the grid at X=2, spanning Z=4 and Z=5. This acts as the brown wooden drive shaft and oil pan, hovering just above the road. The rest of this layer remains empty air.

At Y=1, I will construct the wheelbase and the chassis floor. I must build thick, heavy tires, so I will place double-wide Stone blocks on the outer edges (X=0,1 and X=3,4) at the front axle (Z=2) and the rear axle (Z=7). To protect the vehicle, I will place single Stone blocks at the extreme front (Z=0, X=2) and rear (Z=9, X=2) to serve as bumpers. I will fill the remaining footprint (X=1 to 3) with White Wool to create a soft, carpeted floorboard. However, right in the middle of the cabin at Z=4 and Z=5, I will place Stone blocks at X=2. This creates a transmission tunnel or center console rising up from the wooden drive shaft below, splitting the white wool floor.

At Y=2, I am sculpting the main body of the car. I will pull the width in slightly, ignoring the outer X=0 and X=4 columns where the tires sit. I will use Stone to build a solid 3x3 hood at the front (Z=1 to 3) and a solid 3x3 trunk at the rear (Z=6 to 8). In the center (Z=4 and Z=5), I must create the cabin where the driver sits. Therefore, I will leave the center block (X=2) hollow, placing Stone only on the sides (X=1 and X=3) to act as the car doors. 

At Y=3, I am finishing the build by adding the roof. The front and rear of the car will remain exposed to the air, giving it a sleek profile. I will place a 3x3 square of Stone directly over the cabin area, spanning X=1 to 3, and covering Z=4 through Z=6. This encloses the driver's seat, provides shade, and creates a sturdy rear pillar for the cabin.

PROJECT MISSION: SPATIAL RATIONALE FOR "WATCH TOWER"

1. FOOTPRINT ANALYSIS
I will begin by defining the spatial boundaries. The bounding box for this Watch Tower is 10 blocks wide (X-axis), 11 blocks deep (Z-axis), and 25 blocks tall (Y-axis, from Y=0 to Y=24). Structurally, it is a tiered, mostly hollow build. It features a wide, solid foundation that tapers into a central hollow shaft, bulges outward for a mid-level enclosed observation room, continues as a shaft, flares out significantly into a spacious top deck, and finally culminates in a sloped, pyramidal roof. 

2. MATERIAL STRATEGY
I have selected a specific palette to ensure the tower is both fortified and functional:
- Grass Block (A): I will use this at the very bottom to seamlessly anchor the structure into the natural terrain.
- Stone (B): This is my primary load-bearing material. I will use it heavily in the base and the central core to give the tower a heavy, impenetrable, and fortified presence.
- Oak Planks (C): I will use these for interior flooring, the upper deck platform, and roof supports. Wood provides a lightweight, habitable contrast to the cold, heavy stone.
- Oak Log (F): I will use logs as structural framing, floor joists, and corner pillars. They add visual weight and break up the flat textures of the walls.
- White Wool (G): I will use this in the mid-section walls. In a medieval context, this represents wattle-and-daub or white plaster, making the tower highly visible from a distance as a landmark.
- Glass (H): I will place these in the wool walls to serve as secure, wind-proof viewing ports.
- Stone Slab (E): I will use slabs for subtle exterior overhangs and to create a smooth, gradual slope for the roof.
- Torch (D): I will place these strategically inside the shafts and under the roof overhangs to prevent mob spawns and act as a beacon at night.

3. CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE & LOGIC
Now, I will walk you through the vertical construction, layer by layer.

Base and Foundation (Y=0 to Y=3):
At Y=0, I will lay down a solid 10x11 foundation of Grass Blocks to prepare the site. 
From Y=1 to Y=3, I will construct a heavy, solid Stone base. I will start wide at Y=1, creating a sturdy, slightly irregular footprint. By Y=3, I will step the stone inward. This creates a sloped, reinforced foundation capable of supporting the immense weight of the tower above.

Lower Shaft (Y=4 to Y=6):
At Y=4, I will begin the hollow central shaft. I will build thick Stone outer walls and place Oak Planks in the center to begin the interior floor. The footprint is now roughly 8x8 with cut corners. At Y=6, I will mount Torches on the interior walls to illuminate this lower chamber.

Mid-Level Transition and Observation Room (Y=7 to Y=11):
At Y=7, I will create a structural belt. I will use Stone Slabs on the outer edge to form a subtle overhang, shedding water away from the base. 
At Y=8, I will lay a thick ring of Oak Logs. This acts as a heavy wooden floor joist system to support the room above.
From Y=9 to Y=11, I will build the enclosed mid-level observation room. I will frame the corners with Oak Logs and fill the walls with White Wool. At Y=10, I will insert Glass blocks into the wool to provide 360-degree sightlines. At Y=11, I will cap this room's exterior with Stone Slabs to transition back to the central shaft.

Upper Shaft (Y=12 to Y=14):
I will continue the hollow core upwards. I will mix Stone, Oak Planks, and Oak Logs to create a reinforced, patterned upper neck. At Y=12, I will place Torches inside to ensure the upper stairwell remains well-lit.

The Watch Deck (Y=15 to Y=19):
At Y=15, I will use Oak Logs and Planks to flare the structure outward, creating corbels to support the main deck.
At Y=16, I will lay down a wide 8x8 platform of Oak Planks. This is the primary outdoor watch deck.
At Y=17, I will build a protective parapet ring using Stone and Oak Planks to ensure guards do not fall off the edge.
At Y=18 and Y=19, I will erect Oak Plank pillars on the corners of the deck. These pillars are strictly vertical and will hold up the heavy roof.

The Roof (Y=20 to Y=24):
At Y=20, I will construct the base of the roof. I will create a wide 10x9 overhang using Stone Slabs to protect the wooden deck below from rain. I will also place Torches underneath this overhang to light the deck.
From Y=21 to Y=23, I will step the Stone and Stone Slabs inward layer by layer. Using slabs allows me to create a gentle, tiered slope rather than a blocky staircase. 
Finally, at Y=24, I will place a tiny 2x2 cluster of Stone Slabs to cap the peak of the pyramid, completing the Watch Tower.
